name: 2 Chronicles
author: Jewish tradition credits Ezra, a priest and scribe who helped lead the return from exile in Babylon. Many scholars instead think of an unnamed writer, often called 'the Chronicler', probably a Levite (a member of the tribe that served at the temple) living in Jerusalem. Either way, the writer worked from older records, including the books of Samuel and Kings, and clearly loved the temple, its music and its worship. First and Second Chronicles were originally one book.
audience: It was written for Jews who had come back from exile in Babylon to a small, poor homeland around Jerusalem, ruled by foreign powers. They had a rebuilt temple but no king, and they were asking whether God's promises to David and to their ancestors still held for them.
era: Most scholars date the book to around 400–350 BC, when the Persian Empire ruled the Jewish province called Judah. Jerusalem had been destroyed by the Babylonians in 586 BC, and the Persian king Cyrus later let exiles return and rebuild the temple. Life centred on the temple and its priests rather than a royal court. The book looks back over about four hundred years of Judah's kings, from Solomon to the exile.

notes.3:1: Solomon began building the temple in his fourth year as king, usually dated around 966 BC.
notes.9:1: Sheba is widely thought to have been in southwest Arabia, around modern Yemen, a kingdom grown rich on the trade in incense and spices.
notes.10:1: This meeting at Shechem, an ancient gathering place of the northern tribes, is usually dated around 930 BC, when the kingdom split in two.
notes.12:1: Shishak is the Egyptian pharaoh Sheshonq I, whose invasion around 925 BC is recorded in a list of conquered towns carved on a temple wall in Egypt.
notes.26:16: Uzziah died around 740 BC; the prophet Isaiah began his work around the year of his death.
notes.28:16: The Assyrian king here is Tiglath-pileser III, who around 734 BC was expanding his empire westward across Syria and Israel.
notes.30:1: Assyria had conquered the northern kingdom of Israel around 722 BC, so Hezekiah's messengers were inviting the people left behind in its land.
notes.32:1: The Assyrian king Sennacherib invaded Judah in 701 BC; his own records boast of shutting Hezekiah up in Jerusalem 'like a bird in a cage'.
notes.32:27: The water tunnel Hezekiah dug under Jerusalem, mentioned later in this passage, still survives and can be walked through today; an ancient inscription found inside describes its digging.
notes.33:10: Assyrian records name Manasseh among kings paying tribute to Assyria; his captivity and return are told only in Chronicles.
notes.34:14: This discovery took place around 622 BC; many scholars think the book found was an early form of Deuteronomy.
notes.35:20: In 609 BC Pharaoh Necho II was marching north to help the failing Assyrian Empire against Babylon when Josiah confronted him at Megiddo.
notes.36:15: The Babylonian army under Nebuchadnezzar destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in 586 BC, and many survivors were taken into exile in Babylon.
notes.36:22: Cyrus, king of Persia, conquered Babylon in 539 BC and soon let exiles return home; the book of Ezra opens with these same words.

flags.problem: The note says it is settled that Assyria had already conquered the northern kingdom when Hezekiah sent his messengers. Chronicles places this Passover in Hezekiah's first year, and scholars disagree about when he became king (around 727 or around 715 BC). So it is uncertain whether the invitation came before or after Samaria fell around 722 BC. Assyria had also deported many northerners earlier, around 732 BC.
flags.suggestion: Soften the timing, e.g. 'Assyria had been carrying off people from the northern kingdom of Israel and conquered it completely around 722 BC, so Hezekiah's messengers were inviting those left behind in its land.'
